newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD under pressure now that Kohl to run.
newsitem.headline: German SPD under pressure now that Kohl to run.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision to seek a record fifth term piled pressure on the opposition Social Democrats on Friday to name their own challenger, but the SPD refused to be rushed into battle.

The SPD's rivals to challenge the veteran chancellor -- party chairman Oskar Lafontaine and Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder -- had not even publicly reacted over 24 hours after Kohl announced he would run again next year.
Party manager Franz Muentefering fended off a barrage of journalists' questions with radio interviews insisting the party could wait until April 1998 before picking a candidate.
"We're not going to let them make us nervous, even if (Kohl's announcement) was well presented," he said.
The SPD, in opposition since Kohl wooed its Free Democrat (FDP) coalition into a new centre-right government in 1982, faces a power struggle over its challenger.
Lafontaine, who lost to Kohl in 1990, enjoys more support in the party but puts off centrist voters, the group Schroeder -- though less popular in the SPD -- appeals to most.

While Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) almost unanimously hailed his decision to run again, several of his younger critics in the party hinted their support for him personally did not mean they fully agreed with his policies.

In cautious comments, several of the "wild youngsters" -- CDU state leaders who began openly criticising Kohl's weak leadership on needed tax and pension reforms -- said the party still faced massive problems before the election next October.

"This doesn't mean deference on the issues," said Guenther Oettinger, CDU floor leader in the Baden-Wuerttemberg state assembly. "A party heading into an election year can still have a debate about the issues."

"Now that Helmut Kohl has declared his candidacy for 1998, he has a duty to show more leadership on the issues and get more involved in the debate about the reforms we need," said Peter Mueller, CDU floor leader in the Saar state legislature.
As part of Bonn's drive to meet the Maastricht criteria for Europe's single currency, Kohl has argued that Germany needed an overhaul of its outdated tax and pension systems.
But mounting labour unrest amid record 4.7 million jobless levels has made this daunting task even more difficult, and the chancellor kept aloof from much of the reform debate.
Press reaction to Kohl's announcement was mixed. "The fight has begun!" cheered Bild, the biggest popular daily.
Others were not so impressed. "Kohl wants to again, but who wants Kohl?" Munich's popular Abendzeitung asked, while Cologne's Express said: "Oh, you fat Kohl!"
"Kohl has never risked so much," the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung wrote.
The Berliner Zeitung called his decision "both the best thing and the worst thing that could happen to his party.
"With Kohl, it has a good chance of election success and forces the SPD to make radical leadership choices. But Kohl's new candidacy will prevent overdue reforms taking place."
